utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cucak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In a moment your examination by Mr. Visnjic will continue. What I want to stress to you before it does is that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence on Friday continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe there is a certain degree of vagueness about your testimony last week in terms of the role of the VJ in controlling the state border, the reason being different kinds of systems are used by different countries, therefore I'll be asking you different questions about that just in order to specify. Throughout 1998 and 1999, were the activities of the VJ in relation to the state border implemented in keeping with the laws and regulations that applied?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not just throughout that period. Anything that the VJ did in terms of securing the state border was envisaged by certain laws and regulations and enshrined in those.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about paragraph 5 and 6 of your statement 3D083, did you quote the laws and regulations governing everything to do with the state border for the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Law on Crossing the State Border and the Border Belt I specified those documents as the two fundamental documents based on which all other laws are based.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about Article 48 on the Law on Crossing the State Border and Moving Inside the Border Belt, does that say something of what the powers are of the VJ's border units?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Article 48 of that law says that the border units must secure the state border outside border crossings and settled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. I think it is sufficiently clear why this article refers to controlling the movement of persons outside settled areas. What about inside settled areas? Who exercises control over that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the movement of persons, for example, when there is a settlement, a settled area, that lies at the border itself, this is something that is within the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is the role of the Ministry of the Interior in terms of securing the state border and how is their role different from that of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior secures the state border and controls people crossing at border crossings, crossing into one of the neighbouring countries. It is also in charge of implementing certain laws that are the result of international treaties; for example, violations of the border regime. It is their remit to deal with those violations, as it is of course also of the other units involved in securing state borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, in paragraph 6 where you refer to the rule of the border service and then (item 142), is that a sort of paragraph or section of that rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this is actually an article, but Colonel referred to it as item or paragraph, but it's actually an article. Perhaps we should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 6 of your statement you quote this rule of the border service, item 142?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "item 142," what does that mean? Is that an article or a paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terminology it's called item. There is a chapter, which might contain anything up to 100 items. If you use the other terminology, this would be an article, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that document an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is the same the case with the next one referred to, the directive on documents and reporting, it's not an exhibit? It's just two lines later in the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, that is not an exhibit either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on page 8 of your statement you speak of the border belt and extending the border belt. In which regulation is this possibility envisaged?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matter of crossing the state border is regulated by the Law on Crossing the State Border and Moving Within the Border Belt. These are the laws that tell us about the border belt. It's supposed to be 100 metres of the border itself of the former SFRY, the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia. However, if the services in charge make a special plea to extend it, it can be extended, it's extended but it still remains a border belt. In very conditional terms we then referred to it as an extended border belt. Of course this applied to the area of Kosovo and Metohija and the border to Albania and Macedonia. Earlier on this used to be the case with some other state borders, and that was back at the time of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the VJ made a proposal to the federal government for an urgent extension of the border belt in order to decrease the intensity or reduce the intensity of the terrorists. There should be more involvement in securing the state border in order to put a stop to persons staying in the border belt who do not have appropriate authorisation to be there. Can you please explain briefly to the Trial Chamber how extending the border belt would help bring about a solution to these problems.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that at the outset the border units were only under threat by attacks from Albania and by attacks being carried out by sabotage and terrorist groups that were being infiltrated on a large scale into Serbia and Montenegro, Serbia for the most part, of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, as it was called at the time. These were being infiltrated from Albanian territory in order to bring in weapons and other types of military equipment. At a later stage, when the conditions were in place for the border units to keep these activities at bay, and even more so once the border belt was extended, the sabotage and terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija got closer and closer to the border belt and into the border area itself in order to carry out attacks on bodies in charge of monitoring the situation at the state border and along the state border. I'm talking about the border units of the VJ. In order to keep such activities at bay, firing from Albania and inside their territory, the competent body, having reviewed these problems, made a proposal for a further extension of the border belt, the sole reason being to secure that the border units might get on with their work safely within the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify -- let us clarify this. In addition to attacks and infiltrations from Albanian territory, you also say that there were attacks on the border units from inside, from SFR -- Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia territory -- Kosovo and Metohija, rather; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now return to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have -- I don't see the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you again. In addition, to attacks coming from Albanian territory, the territory of Albania, which included infiltration of groups from Albania into Kosovo, at a later stage there appeared the problem of groups from Kosovo, so from inside, attacking the border units. Is that a fair summary of what you were saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday you testified about this. Heading towards units of the Pristina Corps in November 1998, General Perisic changed his position that he put forward at the 3rd of November collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 3D485 brought up on our screens, page 22, paragraphs 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about the collegium that took place on the 14th of December, 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have page 22, paragraphs 1 and 2. Page 19 of the Serbian, paragraphs 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's fine now. [In English] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please comment. Paragraph 1 of Mr. -- General Smiljanic's contribution, there's a reference being made there to an order by the Chief of the General Staff of the 16th of November, 1998. What is that in reference to?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to link this up with something that I have said already, following the collegium that occurred on the 3rd and the differences in terms of ordering the stepping up of the security system, General Perisic on the 4th, 5th, and 6th went to Kosovo himself in order to see for himself how the security regime along the state border was working. Upon his return from Kosovo, the situation was confirmed that we had already established at the collegium he ordered that appropriate preparations be carried out. He adjusted his previous decision and ordered that a proposal be made in order to step-up the state security regime in the area. It says here that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You don't need to read that, sir, the Judges can see for themselves what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show the witness the same page, paragraph 3, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, before this comes up on your screen, at this particular collegium meeting border-related matters were discussed, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You regularly attended collegiums or collegia of the General Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only when the functioning of the system securing the border state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was concerned; therefore, something from my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you attended this collegium at the 14th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the month or the year for that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 3, the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, just to complete that, your question was, I think the 14th of December, 1998. It was missed in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please look at the last sentence, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please lower the page slightly, pull it down, the Serbian. Further down, please. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an assessment there by General Smiljanic about the number of terrorists in Albania. Let's not go into any details. I want to know about the last sentence under this assessment where there is talk of infiltration, can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this assessment proved to be correct later on. Those terrorist groups that were armed with various weapons, and they also had some weapons they carried with them or on horseback, they infiltrated on rugged terrain where only -- you can only go on foot. And it was our assessment that there were about 250 such places where you could cross from Albania into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 26, paragraphs 3 and 4 of the same exhibit, 3D485, Colonel, this is an intervention by General Marjanovic, where he speaks about the number of troops needed to secure the state border per kilometre, per 1 kilometre. Could you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let me just have a look at it because it's been a long time since I prepared for my evidence. Yes. General Marjanovic presented correct data at that time. At that time a part of our border facing Albania and also parts of our border facing Macedonia were under threat. It was a different situation on the borders with Romania and Bulgaria where we had no problems with the functioning of the security system and there were no incidents there at all. And on this basis he spoke about the number of people needed to -- for the security system at the state border to function properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to you, how many soldiers were needed to secure the state border, if you remember the figure?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember our analysis and assessments. The analysis and assessments were made -- at the time when they were made and on the basis of the situation that existed. According to our assessment between 5.500 and 6.000 people were needed for the system to function at the border between Albania and Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 31 of the English version, that's again the same exhibit, 3D485.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel - well, we'll find it in a minute - could you please look at the first paragraph here right at the top in the Serbian version. This is your intervention, and you are saying that there was a serious incident at the state border. Could you please tell us something about it but very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened at the border post Liken. A serious incident happened there. There was a clash between the terrorist forces and the border people of the VJ, and at the time when the collegium met, I had to report to them to inform them once again about what was happening at the state border. That was at the time when we wanted to save, to protect, the personnel guarding the state border against the terrorist attacks from Albania. There were massive attacks in -- at that time in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the English [as interpreted] text at page 31, the last paragraph, and the first paragraph on the next page, page 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you will have the Serbian version in front of you. This is an intervention by General Ojdanic at this collegium meeting, but before this text appears in front of you could you please tell me what kind of cooperation or what kind of a relationship was there between the border guards and the people who lived in the border area permanently, who were permanent residents there?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before those events, the relationship between the border guards of the VJ and the locals was extremely good, very correct, and often they would come to the commander of the unit securing the border and would inform him about certain events. That was in the period when the situation was stable. As the situation deteriorated, there was a growing resistance among the locals towards the border guards, but there were no border incidents involving the population living in the border area. But according to some rumours that circulated at the time when I visited at the border area, some people told us that they were -- they received threats if they got close with the border guards. So as the situation deteriorated, the relationship between the border units and the locals deteriorated too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the first paragraph in the intervention made by General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Ojdanic was the commander of the 549 Brigade at a certain period of time, and the border relating to some issues was also within his purview as regards the supplying of the border units, replenishment, and so on. And he was familiar with those issues, and he visited the border, state border, often. So he presented the situation in the border units at the border at this collegium. The status of these people, as General Ojdanic said, was really quite remarkable of the people who secured the border and whose relationship with the locals was extremely good, not only in the border belt but in the border area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P1000, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, after this collegium meeting on the 14th of December, some conclusions were made and some tasks issued. Could you please tell us what the collegium concluded and what tasks were issued.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really read it because the letters are too small. I can't remember really, but I know that there was a conclusion to establish an expert team that would analyse the situation at the border with Kosovo and Metohija -- okay, now I see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, it has nothing to do with my question.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would analyse the situation at the border with Albania and Macedonia in the Kosovo and Metohija area and propose appropriate measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This document that is now in front of you, this is an intervention by General Ojdanic at a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council of the 25th of December, 1998, and here General Ojdanic presents some problems and some weaknesses related to the securing of the state border. Could you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version that would be on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Seven features are presented here, or rather, seven salient problems are presented here. Could you please look at them and comment on them. My first question to you is: Did General Ojdanic say anything new in relation to what was discussed at the collegia of the 3rd of November and the 14th of December, 1998 or is it just a summary?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, this is a summary of everything that had already been discussed at the collegia. In fact, most of the -- most important issues had already been raised, issues that affected the functioning of the state border security, and I will not be repeating them because they are stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 3D406.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you said that an expert team had been formed, and once the expert team had concluded its work what were the proposals and what happened with the conclusions of the expert team?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An expert team was established. It included the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army, the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, and another group of experts who dealt with the functioning of the state border security. They studied the overall situation and proposed appropriate measures to improve the state security -- state border security system, and this proposal was of course forwarded to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the federal government accepted those proposals, when it was, and was anything actually done?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proposals were accepted, and one of the documents that the federal government did adopt was the extension of the border belt with -- at the border with Albania, that was on the 3rd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document. Is this the decision of the federal government that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the letters are very small, but yes this is the Official Gazette where this decision was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3D739, that's the map that we have here in front of us. Your Honours, I was told by my colleagues that the key to this map has been translated and it is in e-court. If there are any problems, any ambiguities, it is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please look at the map and explain to us very briefly why the belt is wider in some areas and less wide in other areas at the border with Albania if you look at Montenegro, Kosovo and Metohija, and also the border with Macedonia. If you can just -- you don't have to get up. Could you please do it as you sit.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Let me tell you that the width of the border belt was established in accordance with the assessments of threat. Where there were -- where the threat was higher, where the number of illegal crossings was higher, where there were more terrorists, the belt was wider because this made it possible for the border guards to function in a more safe environment and to operate in greater depth because there were more illegal crossings in those areas, more people crossed illegally, and that was why the belt was defined in those terms. If you look at this map, the belt is wider at the Skadar Lake area at the border with Macedonia because vessels were used to cross the border and to smuggle in all kinds of materials, and if you compare the key to the map with the events that are represented on the map at the border with Kosovo and Metohija, you can see that there -- there is not a single scrap of territory where there had been no incidents involving armed -- fire-arms and where illegal crossings were not attempted. I do apologise, I tend to forget what I have to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In other words, areas where there were more border incidents, the belt was wider?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P640, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I asked you a little while ago how many people were needed to secure the state border with Albania from the territory of Kosovo. Could you please look at this document. This is an assessment of the Kosovo Verification Mission. In particular, could you please look at paragraph 15, which states the total number of personnel needed to secure the border. Could you please tell me, is this a realistic assessment?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would depend on when it was made, but it was very realistic in light of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, do you know that at the Rambouillet talks one of the items on the table was the offer to have 1.500 soldiers guarding the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that this figure was mooted, 1.500 soldiers in -- as far as -- I believe that those soldiers would have been sacrificed had they been used to secure the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to another topic, Colonel. Did you tour the border during the war in -- from March to June 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what did you see there, what was the picture that you formed during your visits?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said last time that this had been an area that was at war, it was a combat zone, and the lives of the people protecting the sovereignty of their state against an outside aggression were at risk all the time. I saw those people who were exhausted who really wanted to protect their territory but who -- who would be on duty for 16 hours. Those people were tired. If you ask them what they wanted, they wanted to get some rest; that was their answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what areas did you visit?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be much better if you asked me which ones I did not visit. I visited all of them. I was head of that particular service, and we toured the border from one end to the other, I and my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please look at 3D741. We are now waiting for that to come up on our screens. Can you please tell us whether during the war there were reports of incidents near the border? How was that procedure being implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just look at this, since I can't see it. Yes. During the war it wasn't only in Kosovo and Metohija that also along all other state borders the state border control regime was reinstated; however, although there was a war on and a state of war had been declared, this was a situation where the state borders were being defended from an act of external aggression, specifically from Albania. I'm waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this exhibit and comment. This is a document produced by the General Staff or the staff of the Supreme Command, and this was sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you straight away, not only did the terrorist infiltrations, attacks, and threats continue, but there was aggression on the territory of Yugoslavia itself. The General Staff was reporting to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at the time about all these things happening within the border belt and at the state border itself. It asked that the domestic public to be informed and that bodies and institutions set up by the General Staff be set up along the state borders. Many such requests were made at the time to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You toured both Morina and Kosova?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both of those border posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of the Serbian, an attack is described there. Who is this carried out by and how?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack here is carried out by sabotage and terrorist forces, an attack on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was a combined frontal attack with incursions from the flanks and enjoying throughout the support of terrorists from the territory of Albania. Their territory was used for heavy firing on the forces and territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Most of these activities were receiving air support from NATO, regrettably. These activities were interwoven with air support by NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see General Ojdanic throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command post. He often came. He toured the units. He reviewed problems. He made suggestions. He gathered information on anything of importance that was happening. He was a true commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The translation says that he often toured the units, and you said he toured the people. Whom did he tour?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both units and people, let me tell you that. These two are difficult to separate. He lived with the people, he toured both the people and the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And all of this was going on where exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout, everywhere. He didn't pick his places. He went to all the most difficult areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And throughout the war, where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question for you, sir. Did you ever hear or were you involved or were you carrying out a plan to expel the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I've never heard of the plan nor did I ever implement this plan which follows I suppose. I don't know that any expulsion occurred at all of the Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're still on your feet, Mr. Visnjic. You're worried that we might not see you. I understand there is some Defence cross-examination. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel. I'm Djuro Cepic. I will ask you questions on behalf of General Lazarevic. I do have a number of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, today you mentioned on page 15 of today's transcript that you toured the entire border or nearly throughout the war in 1999. What I want to know is who welcomed you on behalf of the Pristina Corps when you were off to tour the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excluding the commanders of border battalions, I would often meet and control the state border security regime with General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you in touch with Colonel Zivkovic as well about the border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time he became the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you something about 1998. Did you tour the border units of the Pristina Corps, specifically the 53rd Border Battalion based in Djakovica. Did you go and see them in 1998 specifically?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw all the border units, not just a single border battalion; and when I say "all," that definitely includes the one based in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As of April 1998 and onwards, do you know who unified the involvement of the units of the Pristina Corps in terms of securing the state border to Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, General Lazarevic, he was at the forward command post in Djakovica and I met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Friday's transcript, 14837, this is something you said then and I think you mentioned it today again on page 6 and 7, that the then-Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, on the 4th, 5th, and 6th of November visited Kosovo, went to the forward command post in Djakovica, where he met with the authorities and they told him about the situation and the problems occurring along the state border. My question: Do you know who at the time was in charge of the border forward command post in November 1998? Who reported to the Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic, and convinced him that reinforcements were needed along the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, I do happen to know that. This was General Lazarevic at the forward command post in Prizren at the command of the 53rd Border Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But the headquarters of the 53rd Border Battalion is in Djakovica, right?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djakovica, yes, yes, I'm sorry, I've got it all mixed up. The other one was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking about the security regime along the state border and shortage of forces, could I please have Defence Exhibit 5D1229. Your Honours, this was a document on the 65 ter list, but because of the well-known problems with the CLSS we have not yet received a translation of this document. If I could please ask a single, brief question and for one single sentence to be read from that document, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Up, up -- no down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- You see the heading, you see the stamp. Are you familiar with the stamp?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the command of the 53rd Border Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you show us the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you briefly read this paragraph, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to ensure that there is a possibility of intervention along this axis under threat and assistance to a body under threat, in order to bring up the manpower levels because of those absent, sick, and for replacements to come in, this would require another one-fourth of manpower, which amounts to 300 soldiers and 25 officers. This means that only these axes would be secured over a 24-hour period with no interruption. 1.500 soldiers and 130 officers would be required, which totals 1.630 men. As we speak, the line is being secured by 580 soldiers and 68 officers, which means that another 960 soldiers and 62 officers are missing or we are short of that number of men."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You see the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Major Goran Sorak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 53rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This assessment tallied with your own assessments and the problems were reviewed based on this?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The technical services of the General Staff of the VJ never conducted a single activity on its own along the state border without consulting the border units because they were privy to everything that was going on there and they were always best placed to tell anybody else what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment. Major Goran Sorak was in charge of only a part of the border; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you need clarification of units in the border belt, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- Can direct the witness in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that explains why the numbers are what they are, they are a proportion of the necessary increase in the staff and I just wanted to be clear on that. Does this document now require to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If it is necessary for system, I would like to request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sometimes it's sufficient if the relevant passage is translated in court, but it may be that it's a document -- it's a fairly brief document and the whole of it should be translated. So we will mark it for identification. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask Mr. Registrar to show us Exhibit 5D1227, please. Could you scroll down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you recognise the name and the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sveta Antanasijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 57th Border Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Can you look at 8.5, read that paragraph for us, please?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. "On the 14th of March, 1999, at 1000 hours, in the Globocica border area, three members of the OSCE travelling in a vehicle with the following registration plate number OS 238 MK, the crew comprising Halijev Blajs, Johan Aspont, and Fatmir Iljazi requested authorisation to visit the following visits: Gorance, Globocica, Kotlina, Dragomance. They were allowed to visit."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout the OSCE mission throughout October 1998 to just before the war, what were the conditions that were necessary for the OSCE verifiers to be able to access the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE verifiers under laws could always access the border belt whenever they announced their arrival. They were enjoying an unrestricted freedom of movement as long as they announced their intentions and this document shows just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I said that an announcement was required as well as someone to get in touch with a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, has this document been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not. It is the same problem as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. It also will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Registrar, would you be so kind as to show us 5D1226, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, if you look at the header, do you recognise the unit referred to there?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 57th Border Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you scroll down just for two sentence. Okay, okay, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please read this paragraph after the word "translator," this should be the second paragraph. It says:"Representatives."

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Representatives of the OSCE expressed their satisfaction at the cooperation and changes in the approach to the mission by bodies and units of the VJ. They underlined the fact that the problem of access to the border belt was now resolved and that communication was now established between the mission and the liaison officer. This should guarantee future cooperation. They asked for a map showing the border belt, the 5-kilometre border belt, so that they might be able to get their bearings and announce their arrival."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think you made a mistake in the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, "map," I should have said "map," showing the border belt. My eyesight's not what it used to be; I'm getting on a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My question to you, Colonel, is: Do you know that the OSCE liaison officers expressed their satisfaction at the sort of cooperation they had with the VJ? Is this something you knew about at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. My information suggested that they were very pleased with the way the border units were treating them. We were adamant that they should always announce their visits, lest any accidents occurred. If you don't know who is in the border belt, certain clashes might escalate without you knowing, that's why an announcement was required. It was never a problem of them actually being free to move about within the border belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number 5D1209, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it the last document's also untranslated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that also will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And also this is my last document for tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the same will be the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, would you please tell us what the header says.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of the 55th Border Battalion." My eyesight is really poor, and the document's a bit blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down just to see the signature and the name of -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Major Radomir Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please. That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "A report on a border incident." Could you please tell us who are the addressees of this document, command an so on?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The second passage on this document in front of you: "Command," and then the letters that follow.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command and the local minister of interior, MUP organs, where this battalion was operating, and the local Joint Commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, Colonel. I didn't ask you about the last passage. Could you please look at the top of the screen, the first and the second paragraph, that's what I'm interested, the upper left-hand corner of the screen --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will read it and you comment, please. "Report of the border incident addressed to the command of the PRK (OC and KG) and then OC 3.A and OC ES VJ," could you please tell us what do these acronyms stand for.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's important to stress in those situations where there were serious border incidents the battalion commander addresses this to the Pristina Corps to the operations organ that was to inform the other elements in the system to the operations centre of the 3rd Army that again had to forward this report to other bodies that were supposed to deal with the incident and to the operations centre of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the first few paragraphs of this report so we can see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Tonight at 0015 hours from the territory of Albania from," I can't really make it out, probably sector of their border post Pogaj,"fire was opened on infantry arms at the guard at the Gorozub border post, our organs did not return fire," well I can't really see it,"observed the exact place and took up positions to defend the border post." Just to tell you that this was not the single incident. There were incidents when the facilities around the border post were targeted. We suggested that fire should not be returned but that the whole incident should first be investigated to see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Ask you please slow down for interpretation. Yes, you can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some situations there would be attacks on one axis and then on another axis it would become possible for terrorist teams to be infiltrated and to bring in weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please continue reading the text.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Our organs" -- well, I can't really see what it says here, "to this attack" -- yeah, yeah, okay. "At 0045 hours fire was again opened from the Albanian side to the security detail at Gorozub border post from the same place where the previous attack had occurred. "Our organs returned fire from their infantry weapons, after which the attack ceased" -- well, I can't really see what it says here,"opening fire on our organs. There were no consequences for our organs. This incident we will announce during the day to the MUP organs in Prizren and the local Joint Commission for sector 5." Let me just tell you, for all the border incidents as defined by proper regulations, were always notified to the Ministry of the Interior organs so that the local Joint Commission could then report the incident to the Albanian side and go to the site where the incident occurred. The Yugoslav part of the Joint Commission indicated this to the Albanian side and then they would go to the site. Unfortunately, the Albanian organs very seldom went to the sites of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That would be all, Colonel. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I haven't got any further questions, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, probably I have one more if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just one more question. Throughout the time in 1998 and in 1999, was the chain of command within the Yugoslav Army preserved at all times?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel, my name is Dan Ivetic and I am the attorney for Sreten Lukic and I would have some questions for you, sir. First of all, I would like to ask you some questions about your 92 ter statement. I think the questions will be easily answered without looking at the document but if anyone needs to follow along that would be 3D1083 and the first question I have deals with page 5, paragraph 9 of that statement. Am I correct in understanding the situation that armed incursions by armed ethnic Albanian terrorists was already underway before 1995 on the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were events that were recorded before 1995, and the events escalated in 1995. There was a lull in 1996, and then in 1997, 1998, and culminating with 1999 that was already a large-scale aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I apologise. I'm pausing to allow the transcript to catch up with us, even though I am able to follow your answer as you give it. Now, with respect to these escalations, as you described them, am I correct that at a certain point in time there was actually artillery fire being directed into Yugoslavia from the Albanian territory?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the Albanian territory, it happened many times. I couldn't give you the exact figure. Artillery and recoilless guns and mortars of all calibres were fired from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, I'm just waiting for the translation to come through on the -- pardon me, the transcript, I should say. Now, if I can ask you to clarify another section, page 9, paragraph 2 of your 92 ter statement, wherein you state that the border units registered people illegally crossing the border and handed them over to competent MUP authorities for processing. Did this include those that were attempting to illegally cross the border from Yugoslavia to Albania or to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you right away, those who were caught illegally crossing the border towards the other state outside of the border crossings, they crossed. That cannot refer to the local population that worked and lived in the border belt, because they had full freedom of movement within their place of residence. We couldn't control those locals if they went to their field. So these were not the locals, only those who were outside of their place of residence and locals who were outside of their place of residence who would approach the border or attempt to cross it, but the local population was allowed to work their fields and tend to their cattle and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at page 8 of your statement, it's the last paragraph in the English, you state that the General Staff of the VJ did not receive reports from the MUP during the course of the NATO war regarding numbers of persons who had crossed the border. First of all, I presume you are talking of the MUP in Belgrade and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we received reports from the Ministry of the Interior because it was a federal institution and we were the General Staff. I don't know whether at lower levels they sent reports, for instance, to the Pristina Corps command at the lower level. The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia at the level of the federal Ministry of the Interior did get information about the crossings or -- rather, no such reports were received in war or in peacetime, that was just not practice for such reports to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... To clear something up. I believe -- we're talking about the -- with regards to the border crossings in the territory of the Republic of Serbia and its integral parts, including the province of Kosovo and Metohija, it would be the republican Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and not the federal Ministry of the Interior that would be in charge of the border posts. Is that correct? In the relevant time-period --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- 1998 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by that time there was the subordination within the Ministry of the Interior, within their purview. They would report to the federal ministry supplying the relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you not find all of the answer at line 4 to be confusing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. That's what I was about to go back to, but I want to clear up that issue first to make sure that we're talking about the same things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you talk about the republican Ministry of the Interior being in charge of border crossings, you mean the border between Kosovo and the rest of Serbia, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's your question about -- where are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness has indicated -- talking about the federal Ministry of the Interior and I wanted him to clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but before you do that if you look at the question at line 12: "I believe we're talking about with regards to the border crossings in the territory of the Republic of Serbia and its integral parts, including Kosovo, it would be the republican Ministry of the Interior" -- I mean, what border are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All the borders between the Republic of Serbia and its integral parts with other countries because Montenegro would have its own MUP at the border crossings in that republic at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's what I assumed, but it was just it was indicating something else I thought. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, before I can clear up the first answer, I have to clear up one more item on this last answer that you gave, sir. Just for purposes of the transcript. The transcript records that you said that there was subordination within the Ministry of the Interior, but I thought that in Serbian you said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Could you please clarify with respect to the reporting that you received, was it from the -- was it through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the federal MUP that the General Staff received information.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise if I said the "Ministry of Foreign Affairs," then it really was a slip of the tongue because I served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Let me say again, the republican ministry had to report to the federal ministry on the information and the events within their purview. I did not work in that ministry and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so when you said in response to the question at line -- the answer in line 4 through 11 of page 31 of the transcript, when you said: "That was just not practice for that to be sent," am I correct that the laws and regulations did not envision the Republic of Serbia MUP sending reports directly to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that was not envisaged, although this possibility was not ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Upon request of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the law actually stipulated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to a portion of the testimony you gave today, you talked about the -- and also in your statement at -- in the statement it appears at page 3, paragraph 5 of the English, where you talk about other parts of the border being secured by the responsible forces of the Ministry of the Interior. Now, you have already told us that that would be the border crossings. I would like to ask you if you recall how the laws, the applicable laws, specifically defined the border crossing posts and what activities were to be performed at such posts, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't concern myself with the regulations and laws regarding the border posts, but I know that the border crossing is the place where the state border is crossed and only persons in possession of proper documents were allowed to be there, and that would be the travel documents allowing one to exit or enter the country. In other words, that place and the border belt were within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, and they worked on -- they covered the persons who stay there in the border belt and they controlled the cross -- the people crossing, the border at the border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you describe for us the dimensions or area of the border crossings, any of them if you have any knowledge of Vrbnica, Cafa Prusit, and Djeneral Jankovic, which you say were controlled by the MUP, how large of a space did these border crossings cover?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know the size to the left and to the right of the road, but the dimensions of border crossings may various from 2 to 300 metres up to 800 metres. That would depend on the kind of border crossing and the terrain where it is located. It is not the same for any border crossing, but this is defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can ask you, am I correct that surrounding this limited area of 500 metres or less the VJ had its own units and posts that were in visual sight of the crossings.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it would happen for the VJ to have a line of sight or visual contact. It is not ruled out that they could have been in contact, but it is quite natural for two structures staying in that, securing the border, to contact each other and to agree on the execution of certain tasks in the joint interest that pertain to the state border security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say -- one moment, please. You had said that the persons crossing had to have the appropriate travel documents. At this time I would like to review Exhibit 5D1221, which is a short document. And as we do not have a translation of it as of yet, I will ask you to comment after I read the portion I wanted to direct your attention to so that the American-speaking persons here can know what we're talking about. This is first of all -- I believe it's up on the screen now. Sir, this is a report of the 57th Border Battalion of the Army of Yugoslavia dated the 30th of March, 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th of March, 1999, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to direct your attention to part 4 of this report, and which again I will try to read so that the translators can provide an English translation of the same, and I would ask you just to bear with me and then will have a question after I finish. [Interpretation] "For situation in the territory. "On the 29th of March at 1300 hours, large column of civilian m/vs was noticed moving from Kacanik towards the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. Some of the vehicles crossed the DG and some which did not have the appropriate travel documents were returned." [In English] Now, first of all, sir, for those of us who are not that versed in military acronyms and terminology, what do the abbreviations m/v and DG stand for in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, m/v stands for motor vehicles and DG stands for state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, based on your duties at the -- at the relevant time, in 1999, with the VJ, was it the ordinary course of your duties for you to review such reports from the various border units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away. The General Staff of the VJ received reports directly from its subordinate commands. Sometimes it would happen if the matter of a particular importance or if we had agreed for a report to be sent directly from the border battalion because of its urgency to be copied to the General Staff directly. So most of the reports from the border battalions did not get to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon the documentation and reports that you did review, is this situation illustrated in this report indicative of the typical state of affairs witnessed at the border crossings that persons without travel documentation were not permitted across the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away that the law stipulates that and I believe this is how it was to be done. The border battalion command observed this activity. It did not participate. It observed and it reported. That's quite logical, that's what it was supposed to do, and that's what it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That last document was not used by Mr. Cepic, was it Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was not. It was one of their documents that they have submitted for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it require to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For my purposes it does not. I think the section that I was interested in has been translated in the transcript now it's at Your Honour's leisure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but to get the full sense of this report should it be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The other parts of the report do not deal at all with the same -- with the border crossing. So in terms of my questioning, it does not, but I don't know whether the Lazarevic Defence would require to use the document for some other purpose in which case it would need to be translated. So I defer to my colleague for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you allow me to be useful if we have translation of complete document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that one will be marked for identification. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was the border extended to 5 miles from 100 metres?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight off that we use kilometres as a unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. To 5 kilometres from 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight off, the border was extended many times, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and then all the way to the last extension in March 1999. There were several extensions, extensions. We use the term in a very conditional sense. This is extending the border belt along certain portions of the state border. It can be up to a hundred, but the law says it can be an even greater extension if there is a real need for a greater extension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you now answer the question, please? When was it extended to 5 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, the first time the border was extended was in April. I think there's a document about that, but it was in April, April 1998. That was one extension of the border belt that was ordered by the government I think on the 23rd of April, but the border was extended only facing Albania and not facing Macedonia. Along some sections of the border it wasn't 5 kilometres, but rather less, under 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it there was another extension of the border on the 21st of July, 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the 21st of July. The 21st -- of 1998, well yes. I have the Official Gazette in my brief-case somewhere, the extension of the border belt, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the documents. If we look at 3D406, let's look at page 2 of that document, did this document -- did this decision extend the state border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the area of Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the last decision taken by the federal government to extend the border belt and to establish the border belt more than the previous one, deeper than the previous one. The reason for an extension like this -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So -- I'm just trying to understand your evidence because I thought from your statement you said there was only one extension of the border belt in 1998, and that was on the 21st of July. So we have one on the 5th of March, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before that, there was an extension on the 21st of July, 1998, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 21st, 21st of July, I think so. I would like to see the transcript. I think the 21st of July 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 3D740 -- well, we don't even to look at it. It says the 21st of July - I hope you could accept that from me - 1998 it was extended.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be the 21st of July. I have it in my brief-case, if necessary I can refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So was the decision of the 23rd of April, 1998, published?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, published in the Official Gazette. For any decision to take effect, it must be published in the Official Gazette. You have the conclusions on the last page of the Official Gazette, and then it takes effect and then units can actually use it for practical purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, that decision to extend the border in April 1998, did it -- is that indicated there on the map that you brought, the April 1998 extension?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not indicated, the reason being we only showed the last two extensions. The April extension made it into this bit of the border that is marked yellow. There was no need to make any further indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you understand that answer? Are you saying that the yellow extension on the map is the 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The second-last extension of the 21st of July was marked yellow; the 5th of March one was marked in - what should I call it? - orange. The last two extensions were indicated, but the April extension tallied with the July one. If you look at the April decision, it is quite similar to the July decision. The section of the border was adjusted facing Kosovo and Metohija because that's where the threat was, and in Montenegro it remained virtually the same --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the last part of the witness's question because of the large amount of background noise caused by the shuffling of papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The map that we're looking at shows a yellow extension on the border with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In July when we extended the border belt, it was extended both facing Albania and facing Macedonia. The reason we extended it towards Macedonia was because there were a larger number now of illegal crossings there. At the same time, there were groups that emerged trying to bring weapons into Kosovo and Metohija through Macedonia. They were clocked leaving Macedonia and entering Kosovo and Metohija, bringing in weapons, and that caused us to broaden the border belt so that we might be able in our turn to bring in a greater amount of forces and to exercise more control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Try to confine yourself to what you're being asked. You gave the impression that these two extensions only applied to the border with Albania, and now it seems that the second one also extended to Macedonia. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you saying that the extension of February -- sorry, of April, the 23rd of April, 1998, was an extension of the border facing Albania?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just facing Albania because that border was the border that was at the greatest risk at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when the extension was done in July 1998, that extension was for the border facing both Albania and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, facing both Albania and Macedonia, which is marked in yellow on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what procedures were put in place, if you know, for KVM personnel to visit that extended border area after April of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The KVM were not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Were not there in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They were there much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But they were there after April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring to the border belt that was extended in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- They weren't there in July either --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the relevance to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The date I referred to -- I referred to because the border belt was extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When the KVM were working in Kosovo, what procedure was there in place for them to be able to visit the border belt, as it was extended in July and April?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you about the procedures used by the authorities as far as movement or any stays within the border belt were concerned for any reason whatsoever. I was talking about UNPROFOR at the time. They made regular announcements saying that they would be entering the border belt. They enjoyed unrestricted movement, and you saw the document where they thanked us for it. This was the procedure applied to all those who were granted access to the border belt. They all enjoyed unrestricted freedom of movement whenever appropriate announcements were submitted and appropriate authorisation granted by the relevant bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is what I'm asking about. Did the KVM -- are you saying that the KVM had to follow a procedure of asking for authorisation to enter that border belt that is shaded on the map and they would have to await authorisation before they could enter that area?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. This could be regulated in a variety of ways. I don't know how they did it. I wasn't monitoring them, but you could obtain authorisation for a longer stay in the border belt or for a shorter one. They must have specified the duration of their time within the border belt. They would have been able to obtain permission, they would have been able to move about. If they hadn't applied for authorisation, then they only had the choice of moving about within the border belt in keeping with all the laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't really answer the question. Did they have to ask for permission to enter the border belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know what their position was at the time, but all those moving within the border belt needed authorisation, with the exception of those permanently residing within the border belt. A permit can be a single-entry permit, it can cover varying periods of time, three months, six months, up to a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be convenient, yes. Mr. Cucak, we have to break at this stage for half an hour. The usher will take you from the court and we'll see you again at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Colonel, inquiring about the system, if any, in place to enable KVM members to enter into the border area. Now, I'm asking for what you know; and if you don't know and you have to guess or surmise, just tell us that you don't know and that you're surmising. You spoke about permits. The question is this: If KVM members wanted to enter the border area that you have shaded to make observations, would they have to apply for permits to enter and remain in that area for a fixed period? Do you know of that being a system in place?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they needed a permit or not. I know that under the law any person moving within the border belt must have a permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you're speaking, therefore, not from your personal knowledge of what was required of the KVM if they wanted to enter the border area, but from your view as to what the law provided for?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what the law provided for. I'm not talking about my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cucak, if the border belt was 5 kilometres wide and a person was travelling from Kosovo towards Albania, would that person come to is a check-point at the start of the border belt and then have to go through another one on the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say straight away that it was the Ministry of the Interior that was in charge of border crossings. The roads leading to border crossings were not under control. There was no need to exercise special control there. They would go straight to a border crossing and do whatever they -- their responsibilities were under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, the military or the VJ border units had the power to stop and detain people that they found within the border unit -- the border area to see if they had permits to be within that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border units had the right to stop people and to check their ID. If anything was irregular, they had the power to detain them and hand them over to the Ministry of the Interior.
