Any person moving within the border belt would have an ID on them and they would be able to move about freely. All those permanently residing within the border belt were free to move about unhindered anyway, but they too were supposed to carry ID on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did any KVM member express to you satisfaction with any system for entering and monitoring what is happening in the border area?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another sector in the General Staff that was in touch with them, it was the -- it was not the state border security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it that your answer is no, you did not personally receive from any KVM member any expression of satisfaction with the system for them to enter and monitor the border area?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in touch with them; therefore, I am not in possession of this particular piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were the powers that the army could exercise within Kosovo but outside of the border area in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question. I was dealing with the border service. Ask me something that has to do with the state border, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So you -- I take it you don't know if and what powers the army could exercise within Kosovo if it was outside of the border area?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You stated at -- more than one time -- well, at least one time in your statement that many of the, what you refer to as, terrorist incidents in 1998 constituted an act of aggression against the FRY. In those circumstances of these acts of aggression in 1998, do you, sir, as someone who occasionally attended meetings of the collegium, know if ever it was recommended that a state of emergency be declared in Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I attended collegium meetings only when they had to do with the state border; other than that, I did not attend any meetings. As soon as discussion was over on this specific subject, I would leave the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So was it ever suggested or proposed that these border incidents which you said were acts of aggression against the FRY in 1998 were good reason for a state of emergency to be declared in that area? Was that discussion ever raised while you were at any meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This wasn't what I was there to discuss, although there were a great many acts of aggression and I think there are documents to show just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you went through item by item I believe but you went through the various incidents that were referred to in the White Book that was published by the Yugoslav Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Did that -- did the White Book cover incidents and events in which the Yugoslav Army attacked KLA positions and caused casualties among members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I found to be of interest in the White Book were the incidents mentioned in it; however, only selected incidents based on the -- a selection made by the author were included. A lot more than just those had occurred, and you can find that in the records of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For example, we heard evidence that during the summer to autumn of 1998 in the course of a VJ offensive in that period, thousands of KLA members were killed, that is not represented or that is not covered in the White Book, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I just looked at the incidents. When I saw an incident involving border posts and the border area, I looked at that. But believe me, I didn't go through the whole book --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- As a professional dealing with that sort of thing, I knew what those incidents were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What do you mean when you said that General Ojdanic toured the people? Maybe the translation I have or had is not precise, but that is the translation I have.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Ojdanic was acting as a man who was there to go and see the people, see his subordinates, to see what problems they were encountering, what their problems were both in personal and professional terms, and he was one of the high-ranking officers who saw every human being in a larger overall context and attached appropriate importance to each and every human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So when you said he toured the people, you mean he toured the VJ -- he went and visited the VJ personnel in the various units?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While -- well, do you know if in 1999 during the time of the conflict, that's from March 24 or thereabouts to mid-June, he toured Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't know when General Ojdanic was in Kosovo because that was not within my domain, following him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just asked you because you said that he went everywhere.

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went everywhere to various units, I'm speaking about him in general terms. He went to units when he felt the need to go somewhere earlier on and as Chief of General Staff. The example with the border, that speaks in itself, while he was still brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know which command posts he went to? Your evidence is earlier that he went to the command post a number of times or he went there often. Which command post or posts were you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Chief of General Staff, it wasn't only General Ojdanic, other chiefs of General Staff, too, went to the command post of the 3rd Army, the command post of the Pristina Corps, to the forward command post of the Pristina Corps that existed in Djakovica. That is the command posts that I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So General Ojdanic during the conflict toured a command post in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was at that command post. General Ojdanic should be asked that. I know that I was in charge of the border, and when it was a question of the border I personally went there. Whether he was in Djakovica during the conflict, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At least it's friendly conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, during the course of your testimony today, when I asked you where it was that you saw General Ojdanic during the course of the war, you said at the command post. Can you say where this command post was, where you saw General Ojdanic during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADE CUCAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him at the command post of the staff of the Supreme Command in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cucak, that completes your evidence; thank you for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's Negovan Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Sepenuk on behalf of General Ojdanic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic, good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 you were a colonel in the Yugoslav Army --

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, sir, I have a problem with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think you'll be helped.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear every now and then, there seems to be something wrong with the wiring. [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You were a colonel in the Yugoslav Army in 1998 and 1999; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way there's a full colonel and a lesser colonel, you were a full colonel, I take it?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you retired from the army in 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what's your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You retired?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And -- okay. And what do you do in your retirement, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Enjoy life in the country, rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Far away from military service?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And you own a couple of horses, correct, and that takes a lot of your time? You have to say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you retired in 2003, correct? And I want to summarize --

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- Your army service, I want to summarize your army service from the time you graduated from the military academy. And when did you graduate from the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with your permission and I take it no objection from the Prosecutor may I just do some brief leading questions to get his background in the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No objection, it's been leading already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We're in an early stage of the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I take it in 1973 following graduation from the academy you joined the army security service - and stop me if I'm incorrect on any of this - you joined the army security service, you took a break for three months in 1976 to attend language school in London, and spent one year in 1977 in London at the staff military college school of command and control. Is that correct? You have to say yes or no. Is that correct to this point, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to just pause here for one moment because to me, Colonel - and we've met obviously before you testified - you speak and understand English fairly well, but I understand that you are more comfortable in responding to my questions in your native Serbian language. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And getting back to your background, you became a liaison officer in Belgrade with the Foreign Liaison Service, and then from 1983 to 1989 you were an intelligence desk officer in Belgrade. You spent 1989/1990 in Angola as a member of the verification mission there and then four years in Ankara, Turkey in the Yugoslav Army as an attache to the ambassador, correct, military attache?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you became the deputy chief of the Foreign Liaison Service as I understand it in 1994, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then you became the chief of that service in 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture now on your history, as I understand it that you also spent some time with the OSCE right before you retired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was your position at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was military advisor to the ambassador, who was representative to the mission of the country to the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, getting back to 1994, Colonel, when you were the deputy chief of the Foreign Liaison Service, I want to direct my questions to this area now. It will be a little more tradition in our questioning now. What is the Foreign Liaison Service? Please tell the Trial Chamber what it is, what it does, what are its duties?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Foreign Liaison Service with -- for cooperation with international organisations is set up by the General Staff and its task is to communicate on a daily basis with foreign military representatives and to look into possibilities of promoting inter-army cooperation with representatives of the countries represented. Among others, the task -- one of the tasks of that office was to take care of all the needs of foreign representatives in the country in terms of resolving all problems related to their accreditation, functioning, accommodation, up to their very private problems, like their children's education, medical care, and so on. As I said, it's a day-to-day job and through this communication the task was to provide information about the life and activity of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, Serbia now, and in this way to make it possible for all foreign military representatives to obtain the best possible information in order for them to adjust and to communicate with the representatives of the army in terms of carrying out the tasks put before them by their own armed forces, or rather, ministries of defence, that would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you dealt with the military attaches of the various countries? You have to say yes or no. You have to answer audibly.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you recall the number of countries involved just offhand, 20, 25 countries, thereabouts? Just tell us what your rough estimate was of the number of country military attaches you dealt with.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, I think it was 23 or 25 countries, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how many employees did you have in the Foreign Liaison Service that you supervised?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The number varied, but as a rule between 15 to 20 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did your duties change at all when you became chief of the Foreign Liaison Service in December 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, no, but I took over full responsibility for the work of the office now, thereby extending my work, that is to say financial in other duties that were indispensable for the normal functioning of an independent agency such as the Foreign Liaison Service is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel, when did you first meet General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was when he became Deputy Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the record shows that that was in June of 1996. Does that jibe roughly with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in principle -- well, I do not recall the exact date, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In any event, you met him when he became the Deputy Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what were your contacts with General Ojdanic after he became the Deputy Chief of Staff, just summarize them for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the initial period while I was still deputy head of the office, these contacts were rare, only when the head of office was absent, because communication with superiors always went through the head of the office. From the moment when I became head of the office, that communication was practically on a daily basis. I directly reported to the deputy chief about all matters of interest to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Army of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So after General Ojdanic became the Chief of Staff - and that was in November of 1998 - you had frequent contacts with him, more frequent contacts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After General Ojdanic became the Chief of General Staff, these relations continued, but not as frequently, only at his request. Since subordination regulates that the head of office directly carries out his communication with the General Staff with the deputy Chief of General Staff. So that continued in this particular case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. And -- so while he was Deputy Chief of Staff you had frequent contact with him, almost daily. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Would you call him in the mornings? Would you talk to him in the mornings when the day first started; and if so, tell the Chamber about it, please?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whenever there was a reason for that, the Deputy Chief of General Staff had to be informed about possible requests of foreign military representatives that were addressed to the General Staff and that pertains to possible meetings, requests for meetings, receiving certain information about the activities of the Army of Yugoslavia, and similar matters that were of interest for the foreign military representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you had numerous contacts with General Ojdanic, both when he was the deputy chief and the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And from your frequent interactions with General Ojdanic, Colonel, could you tell the Trial Chamber, give them some sense of General Ojdanic's qualities as both a military commander and as a human being.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, General Ojdanic is an exceptional professional, open, direct, tolerant. As a person, sociable, a sense of humour, again direct in his communication. If he likes you, he'll tell you straight away; if he doesn't, he'll say that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: An open, direct man?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And there's an expression: What you see is what you get. Did that or did that not apply to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, after you became head of the Foreign Liaison Service in December 1997, would you attend meetings of the collegiums of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I was invited to attend, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you attended those meetings not all the time, but as I understand it quite frequently - is that a fair statement - quite regularly?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And generally what happened at these meetings and who attended them?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see from the very name of this body, the collegium consists of all the assistants to the Chief of General Staff according to all the arms and services. The direct associates who are indispensable for daily assessments of the situation in terms of what was going on in the army and making decisions pertaining to life in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And how would you describe the atmosphere, the mood, of these collegiums?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Like any other meeting, meetings of the collegium have a certain agenda envisaged for a particular day. Therefore, the atmosphere, in a way, varied from one meeting to another. In principle, the atmosphere was a working atmosphere, open, correct, and tolerant. There were open debates about all the issues that were on the agenda for that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I take it differing viewpoints were expressed by the various persons attending the collegiums?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was there a free and fair and frank exchange of information on even the most controversial of issues?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did General Ojdanic in your recollection ever impose restrictions of the debate, try to cut people off and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, no; however, it could happen if somebody would expand on a particular topic or present without arguments some information or if one diverged from the topic in an inappropriate way, there certainly were such cases when the floor would be taken away from someone during the course of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So if somebody talked too much, General Ojdanic would sometimes say, That's enough; is that a fair way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, at any of these collegium meetings, Colonel, did you ever hear any talk whatever of a plan to expel the Kosovar Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Aside from these meetings, Colonel, did you ever hear General Ojdanic at any time talk about expelling the Kosovar Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did General Ojdanic ever do anything or say anything that indicated that he was prejudiced against the Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that's all I'm asking you. Not that you know of, correct? And Colonel, when -- I say "not that you know of." Did you ever consider him prejudice in any way against the Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall the agreements in October of 1998 setting up the OSCE verification mission?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We've had extensive testimony in this trial about that, but I wanted to know what was your role, if any, in this verification process?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this commission was at the level of the government and the agreement was signed at the level of the government, the office for relations with foreign military representatives only offered some assistance to our authorities in terms of preparing people, providing translation/interpretation services, and sending so-called liaison officers that facilitated contacts, prepared contacts, and helped with interpreting. That is all that the office did from that point of view in relation to fulfilling those tasks of the Federal Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And directing your attention to November 27, 1998, Colonel, did you and General Ojdanic and others meet with General Drewienkiewicz - by the way we call him General DZ, you know who I'm talking about, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you meet with General Ojdanic and others, did you meet on that day with General DZ and others?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do you recall that that was pretty much the first day that General Ojdanic was on the job and a day he also attended the November 27th, 1998, collegium? He did both that day, he attended the collegium and he went to this meeting. Do you have any recollection of that; if you don't, that's fine, but I'm asking you now whether you do?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that it was right at the beginning of his time as Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you. And you -- as I understand, you helped to prepare the agenda for this meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And the meeting was called by General DZ, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was at their request that the meeting was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, with respect, we could proceed without leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: There's also been extensive testimony on this by General DZ who said he called the meeting, but that's fine, Your Honour, I'll make an effort to be more direct-like in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, by the way, had you met General DZ before?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: When did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1978, we went to the staff officer's school together in the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that was -- that was a -- how long was that staff officer's school? How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: A year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was General DZ's rank?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So you saw him frequently during that one-year period, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Were you surprised to see him 20 years later, at this is November 28th, 1997, meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what was his reaction and your reaction when you first laid eyes on one another?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we recognised each other although it had been 20 years. We exchanged greetings in a quite cordial manner. We hugged each other, if that means anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, did you take notes at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And are your notes reflected in Defence Exhibit 3D438?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If we could put that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You can look, Colonel, at either the Serbian or the English version, whichever you're most comfortable with, probably the Serbian version. And are those -- is that a copy of -- a summary of your notes, that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is it, in your opinion, an accurate summary of what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who were the people -- if you'll look in footnote 1, don't name everybody. I just trying to give the Trial Chamber a sense of who was there. Just look at footnote 1. Who were one or two of the people who attended the meeting -- along with General Drewienkiewicz --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Your Honour, again with your indulgence and Mr. Stamp's, just to save a little time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Was one of the persons attending the chief of the OSCE office in Belgrade Major General Pellnas, right? Did he attend?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear if you look at this footnote. We always took down the composition of both delegations, all the relevant OSCE representatives in Kosovo and Belgrade were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And General Obradovic was there for the VJ and others, correct? We'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, again the Trial Chamber can read this document, so just tell us briefly, Colonel, what happened at this meeting in one or two sentences.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As we set at the outset, the meeting was first requested by the representatives of the verification mission, the objective being to review all the possibilities as to how the task of the verification mission in Kosovo would run as smoothly as possible. It was also important to deal with any problems that might have emerged up to that point. Overall, the objective of the meeting was to ensure that the OSCE mission would not encounter any hindrances in its work, and that is what the meeting came down to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And there was an exchange of views on various subjects, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And during the discussions, was there some disagreement about the interpretation of the October agreements; and if so, can you recall an example?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the only disagreement or potential disagreement was about interpreting the methods of the OSCE verification mission, the methods that it would use in its work. According to the agreement, they were supposed to conduct verification pursuant to provision 4 of the Dayton Accords on weapons control, on subregional weapons control. And according to one interpretation, there was no need to verify the army as such, but the OSCE requested unconditional access to all military facilities and units in Kosovo. I think this was the only stumbling block, as it were, in the interpretation of the agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So one difference was the OSCE wanted to go into the military barracks; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And if you would look at just one paragraph in 3D438, and it's on page 3 of the English version and just in the interests of clarification, Colonel, if you wouldn't mind looking at the English. It's the third paragraph -- third page, I'm sorry, third page, third paragraph, 3D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If the usher would put that up, please. That's the Serbian. Can we have the English, please. That's right. If you blow up the -- that's right. Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So that paragraph -- it's -- it says: "In response to Colonel Marjanovic's" -- who's Colonel Marjanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I remember, he was a representative of the subregional arms control committee, which was the body within our army which was in charge of implementing provision 4 of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So to go on --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honours, this is the only paragraph I'm going to read from this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It says: "In response to Colonel Marjanovic's observation that the Agreement does not define the admittance of OSCE Mission members into barracks, General Drewienkiewicz pointed out that the Agreement clearly states unlimited freedom of movement and access without exception. He would carry out the verification where and when he wishes, according to his own decision and possible prior notification by telephone about his arrival at a specific barracks." That's the paragraph. And I ask you, Colonel, do you have a comment about that?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing special. This is typical of Drewienkiewicz, to put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what do you mean by that "typical of Drewienkiewicz"?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my experience of socialising with him for a year, we have an expression in our language for that, he always needs to have the say. Whatever he decides will eventually be done; that's his attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. A bit abrasive; is that a fair statement? General Drewienkiewicz, a bit of an abrasive man sometimes?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say abrasive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in any event, despite this disagreement or some disagreements in interpretation, how would you characterise the tone and the mood of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The mood was that of achieving an agreement and avoiding any misunderstanding in terms of making it possible for the mission to go about their duties in a smooth and unhindered manner. This means that our side took every step to reduce any problem to a minimum or to remove it altogether so that the mission might continue its work. It did happen that we had to harmonize our positions on certain matters, which in turn made it possible for us to avoid any further misunderstandings in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But by and large, a friendly, cordial meeting; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, an open one, even creative I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And at the end of that meeting in your notes here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Forgive me, Your Honours, I have to break my promise, two more lines -- four more lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- At the end of your notes you say that a public statement was issued after the meeting and this appears, I'll just read it. There's no dispute about it. "Both parties emphasised the significance of the verification process as a condition for resolving the problems in Kosovo and Metohija by political means. The Chief of the General Staff expressed the determination and willingness of the Yugoslav Army to realise its obligations within the process of verification consistent." Do you remember that being in there? We've gone over this before. Am I quoting correctly?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And subsequent to this meeting of November 27, 1998, from your association with General Ojdanic, Colonel, what was his position from then on out on cooperation with the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the minutes clearly show that we and General Ojdanic, above all, as Chief of General Staff, as well as the entire team, had the firmest resolve not to do the least thing that would stand in the way of the OSCE inspection's work. If that had not been the case, we would have caused ourselves a lot of harm. We did everything within our power for the mission to continue its work in a smooth and unimpeded manner. There was no question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honours, I had marked as an exhibit a letter from General Drewienkiewicz to General Ojdanic of 2 December 1998, thanking him for being at the meeting and thanking him again for cooperation, that kind of thing. And I found out in preparing for the witness that this exhibit has already been admitted, it's Prosecution Exhibit 2543, and so there's really no need to introduce 3D437.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And this letter I'm talking about, Colonel, is December 2nd, 1998, letter from General DZ to General Ojdanic thanking him for his cooperation. As I understand it, you heard about this letter but never saw it because you were in the hospital recovering from surgery, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to probably our last subject, when did you first meet Colonel John Crosland?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that I can't remember the exact date, but it was since his first arrival in Belgrade as a representative of Great Britain that we were working together. So I could say that we were working together from the very first time he arrived as an envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And we've had testimony from Colonel Crosland and his statement, which is P2645, and he got here -- he got to Belgrade August of 1996. So I take it then you had frequent contact with him from August 1996 to 23 March 1999; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And under what circumstances would you see Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: What condition our meetings were instructions on the protocol in dealing with foreign military envoys. The sector itself was in charge of regulating the life and work of military envoys. They spoke to our administration every time they had a problem with their life or work in Belgrade. Starting from day one, that is, introductions being made to the administration. Unlike ambassadors, envoys don't -- do not present credentials. They present themselves to the appropriate administration, and that is what they do on day one of their stay in the country, and from there on, depending on their requests and how frequent they are, communication can be more or less intense. Sometimes it can be daily. It really all depends on the kind of problem being encountered by a military envoy. It can also depend on the interest of our army in relation to a particular foreign military envoy. This communication was not as intense with everyone; it varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But you had pretty frequent interactions with Colonel Crosland during a long period of time, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And did you have a good relationship with Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, full respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you met with him not only professionally, but as I understand it socially, correct?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, but it wasn't just he. This applied to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. When I questioned Colonel Crosland at this trial on February 8th, 2007, I'm mistakenly referred to you as General Jovanovic, that's on page 9908 of the record. Colonel Crosland corrected me at that time and he said: "I wish they had made him a general. He was a very good friend." Do you agree with Colonel Crosland, were you in fact good friends, very good friends?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: We understood each other quite well. In our line of work, you have to be able to make a distinction between your life as an officer and private issues. If you can abide by that distinction, then you have no problem in dealing with people regardless of how different or opposed your official positions might be. Our role was to keep the door open all the time to communication with these people. Therefore, if someone says we were friends, I would be rather prone to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And -- but I take it then even though you became friends or good friends, I take it you would occasionally have your disagreements with Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: By all means, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, when you met with Colonel Crosland, did you sometimes make a memorandum of the meeting, take notes and then reduce it to a memorandum; did that sometimes happen?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. Whenever something of interest to the army was being discussed, a note was drawn up and submitted to the relevant offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And is 3D511 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's already in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: -- 3D511 your summary of the notes that you made of a meeting with Colonel Crosland on June 25th, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If we could just put that up on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think all you'll have to do is look at the first page. It's in Serbian, that's fine. It's in B/C/S. Is that the meeting I'm referring to and did you take notes at that meeting and did you summarize your notes which are in a document now called 3D511?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Notes are always drawn up. I'm not sure if I drew these up myself or one of my assistants, but I'm sure that this is the thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: But I take it, it was based on notes that you made at the meeting, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And at my request, you've looked at this exhibit prior to trial and are you satisfied that this is an accurate summary of what took place at that meeting with Colonel Crosland?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Colonel Crosland at the trial at page 9909 has already testified to the accuracy of portions of this summary and there's been testimony about it, so I'm not going to ask you any more questions other than one, Colonel, and that is: Does this exhibit, 3D511, generally contain Colonel Crosland's comments about the dangers posed by the KLA and how the Yugoslav Army should react to those sets of dangers in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is the essence of the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to 27 August 1998, did you attend a briefing of the foreign military attaches in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And by the way, how frequently did such briefings occur in your experience, as both the deputy chief of the FLS and the chief of the FLS, how frequently over a several-year period would these meetings occur?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, once or twice a year, but if more than that was required there could have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who would usually be the lead briefer? Who would brief the foreign military attaches on behalf of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It very much depended on the subject matter being discussed with military attaches. Those doing the informing were the relevant persons, assistant Chief of the General Staff, heads of the security administration, and sometimes the deputy Chief of the General Staff, if that is what the Chief of the General Staff wanted. It could have been any of the assistants. It all depended on the subject matter under discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Colonel Crosland has testified at this trial that, like you, he also attended this August 27th, 1998, briefing. And he also testified that following this briefing he gave you a video of the VJ which showed the shelling of Suva Reka and other areas. And I ask you now, Colonel: Did Colonel Crosland ever give that video to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he give it to anyone on your staff?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Did you make an effort to learn whether Colonel Crosland may have given it, if not to you, then to some member of your staff; and if so, tell us about those efforts.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Early that year when a request was submitted to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. When you say "early that year," do you mean this year, early in 2007?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you said a request was submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And who made that request?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think someone on the behalf of Mr. Visnjic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally couldn't remember. It was only natural that I tried to go back to the administration, we used to be the administration, and search in their files for this document. This document would have been recorded if this document was ever received, a note would have been drawn up on it, but we couldn't track it down. We found no paper trail, no trace of that document ever having been received by anyone in the administration. Secondly, I tried to get in touch with the people who were in my office at the time, including the translator. I tried to ask them if they remembered coming across anything like that, and no one could say. We simply couldn't track it down. We couldn't find anyone who in any way laid eyes on that kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Jovanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. Any Defence cross-examination? Mr. Jovanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown a document, 2D438 [sic], which is your record of a meeting involving General Ojdanic, General DZ, and others. And it says here, sir, that General Ojdanic - and this is at page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think it should be 3D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic, I think that's correct, 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Ojdanic promised that the VJ would implement the provisions of the agreement and Security Council Resolution 1199 and that it would deliver reports on the arrival and departure of units and troops in Kosovo and Metohija for the purpose of the exchange. Do you know, sir, of troops from outside of Kosovo being mobilised and brought into Kosovo in January, February, March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. That was never within my line of work. My line of work had to do with a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we have evidence that there were various units and formations brought into Kosovo in that period of time and that no reports were made by the VJ. Would you be able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to your meeting with General -- with Mr. Crosland - and that's August 27, 1998 - Mr. Crosland said that he handed over the video across the table perhaps to you or one of your staff. Can I ask you this: Did you try to contact your staff members and ask each of them if they had received this tape because you recognised the possibility that it might have been received by one of them but was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that it was possible that someone had received -- actually, I'm saying that it is not possible for someone to have received some material without there having been a written record of that. Secondly, Mr. Crosland could not have given anything to anyone across the table because at this table where a person sits during the briefing or during the meeting or whatever, there's only three or four people sitting there, including the interpreter, so everything can be seen. And thirdly, it was not customary for any of the military representatives or military attaches in front of all the other envoys that were in the same room to carry out any kind of exchange of information in writing or in any other way. This, quite simply, is not in accordance with the principles governing the work of military representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why is it in 2007, this year, that you asked as many staff members as you could find whether or not they had received the video? Why was it necessary to go and ask them?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was necessary because when you advocate a certain position after so many years, quite simply, you have to check out all the possibilities because it is impossible for someone to remember such details from communication with foreign military representatives that was practically on a daily basis with all. You have lots and lots of meetings with other people, too, not only with one man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your question was: Why is it in 2007 you asked as many staff members as you could find? Did the witness say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm paraphrasing the witness. I think the witness said that he made inquiries of staff members or interpreters, et cetera, in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that correct, you made inquiries of your staff members, including your interpreters, this year, in 2007?

utterances.speaker: NEGOVAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, that completes your evidence; thank you very much for coming to give it. You can now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall adjourn now and resume at 20 minutes to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.39 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your next witness, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our third witness is General Milorad Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is going to be a live witness, and we will try to stick to the four hours envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of General Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, for the transcript, can you give us your name and profession.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I am Milorad Obradovic, born in 1942 in Montenegro. Now I am a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What rank did you have when you were pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: My professional service in the Army of Yugoslavia ceased when I was a colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you describe your military career to the Trial Chamber, the posts you held?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: After completing the national defence school, I had the following duties: Brigade commander, chief organ in the corps command, Chief of Staff and corps commander, Chief of Staff of the 2nd Army, assistant Chief of General Staff for the operation staff sector, commander of an army, and my last duty was the assistant Chief of General Staff for ground forces and that is when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When were you retired, General?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was retired in 2001, towards the end of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What post did you hold in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1998 I was sector chief of the 2nd Army, and from the end of July I came to the General Staff as assistant for the operations and staff sector, and I remained there until the end of March 1999. Then I became commander of the 2nd Army until the end of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We're going to start with when you became assistant head of sector for the operations and staff activities. You said that that was in the first, or rather, the end of July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the second half of July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as for this post you were directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I was one of the assistants to the Chief of General Staff, who was directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who was Chief of General Staff at that time, General Perisic, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: General Perisic was then Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say the sector for operations and staff activities, can you explain to the Trial Chamber what the main functions were of that sector?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The sector for operations and staff activities was an entity within the General Staff. Its structure was the following: It had its first administration, the fifth administration or the financial one and an arms control division in accordance with the Vienna Agreement on Arms Control. The basic function of the sector was, or rather, the primary function of the sector was that of planning. Furthermore, finance which regulated the overall financing of the Army of Yugoslavia and, as I said a few moments ago, there were the tasks stemming from the Vienna Agreement on Subregional Arms Control in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We are now going to dwell on the function of planning. What did it contain?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It contained primarily the elaboration of certain plans at the level of the General Staff, directives, and orders regulating the way in which assignments were being carried out in the army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, which plans were elaborated in your department in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The General Staff as a whole elaborated the more important plans. The sector for operations and staff activities particularly elaborated special-purpose plans, that is how we defined them. These plans include the following: The plan of use or, as somebody calls it, the war plan; then the plan of developing the army, the plan of equipping the army. Various orders and directives were drafted regulating the mode of implementation of various tasks. There were also other plans that accompanied the realisation of these major plans; however, as far as our sector was concerned these were the more important plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, who approved these plans after your sector elaborated them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The sector as a whole was not working on these plans alone, it was the General Staff as a whole; however, the sector participated at the level of the domain of its own work. These plans were approved by the Chief of General Staff, the more important plans, that is, those resolving system-based issues, like the plan of using the troops, mobilisation, equipping the army, financial plans, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who approved what you called the war plan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The plan of use, or the war plan, was drafted and then sent to the Supreme Defence Council; that is to say, the top echelons of the state. And when approved, it was approved by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to the General Staff, in the second half of July 1998, I assume that you were made aware of the existing plans?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: One of the principal obligations that I had, since this was the first time I came to work for the General Staff, to familiarise myself - how should I put this? - with the overall situation within the sector, what the important tasks were that were topical then, what orders and plans were being elaborated, and what the sector and its organs focused on at the time. These plans, or rather, tasks were indicated to me by my associates, the chief of the first administration. As for the planning function, then the head of the fifth administration in terms of financing the army, and the head of the head of the department for control focused on the tasks in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who was head of the first administration at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: When I came, General Smiljanic was head of the first administration, and he remained there throughout while I was chief of sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what plans existed then in the first army, or rather, in the first administration?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The first administration, as I said, focused on planning, the planning function. In addition to the war plan, or the plan for use, and the development plan, the plan of equipping the army, the operations plan, then operative masking, then the annual plan. Those were the basic plans, also tours envisaged from our own line of work and the rest that accompanied these more important plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Special-purpose plan, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Special-purpose plans -- excuse me. Special-purpose plans are these unique plans. That was the so-called plan for use or the war plan. Then mobilisation development plans, because it wasn't that they -- there were several of them; that is why they're called special-purpose plans. There was also an order that regulated everyday life in the troops that was called the order on special measures related to constant combat-readiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This order on measures related to constant combat-readiness, from when had that been in existence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That order had been in existence from earlier on, considerably earlier on. It was drafted by the General Staff but it was also worked on in subordinate commands. It was updated from time to time when necessary, but as a rule annually, the beginning of the year or when necessary. I said that it was done at the level of the General Staff, and it was sent to subordinate commands and units; and all the commands down to brigade level worked on that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, General, what it actually represents, what are these measures related to constant combat-readiness?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This order regulated everyday life; that is to say, the implementation of everyday tasks in a planned fashion in wartime and in peacetime and carrying out tasks that were everyday tasks, namely, training, securing facilities, borders, combat-readiness measures. In a way, if I can put it that way, this is day-to-day activity in units and commands that were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what does this mean, "measures of combat-readiness"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the overall situation that existed in zones of responsibility. There were measures that were envisaged, and then in accordance with the previously mentioned order units had certain levels of combat-readiness within a certain duration. Some had three-hour combat-readiness, some had six-hour combat-readiness, and some even longer than that; that is to say, depending on the situation and the circumstances that they would find themselves in so that they could successfully carry out their tasks within the period of time that was set for the implementation of their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me try to simplify matters. Does that mean that if a unit has an order for the six-hour combat-readiness measure, does that mean that it has six hours from the time that an order for a task to be carried out is issued to get to such a level of readiness to actually carry out the task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in principle that's what it is. If a unit is in a peacetime status and it has the three-hour or six-hour combat-readiness time, so if a task is received or if a situation occurs, this unit has to be ready within six hours to carry out the task. Now, maybe a facility is at risk or a situation occurs at the border, something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are those plans done in all units, or rather, orders, the orders for constant combat-readiness, are they done at all levels in the chain of command in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said this order was issued by the General Staff. It was further elaborated at army commands, at corps commands, brigade commands, and further down the chain of command, where it was regulated down to the smallest detail the tasks for each and every unit. I'm sorry. It pertained to the use of peacetime formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were the sector chief, that was from the second half of July until the 2nd of April, or rather --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The end of March, in addition to the existing plans that you just described to us, what other plans were drafted at the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that when I got to the General Staff, I acquainted myself with the overall situation and the purview of activities of the sector and partially also with the other tasks that the other sectors dealt with. This situation was analysed often at the level of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff on the basis of monitoring the overall situation, the tasks that the army or some of its units had, assessments of the situation were made and the Chief of General Staff ordered that the tasks be carried out in accordance with his orders. And this was all elaborated in various orders that were in force at that time at the lower levels of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us, my question was: What other plans were made? Could you please tell me what plans were made at the time when you were in this post at the level of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 in late July, the Chief of General Staff ordered inter alia that a plan be drafted that we use the code-name Grom 98, Thunder 98. It doesn't mean a thing, it's just a code-name. And pursuant to this order a directive was drafted that had this title for further action and the execution of tasks in the military as a whole with the focus on tasks to be carried out by the 3rd Army. That plan had two stages --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I apologise. Could you please tell me, in addition to this plan, Thunder 98, in the course of 1998 and 1999, did you draft any other plans?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999, in late January, another plan was made, its name was Grom 3, Thunder 3, at the level of the General Staff and the tasks were regulated by a directive issued by the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now go back to Thunder 98, that plan. How was this directive drafted, the directive called Thunder 98? Who issued the order to do so?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the way that the General Staff operated at the time, at the collegium of the Chief of General Staff the overall situation was analysed, I mean the situation in the country, in the Army of Yugoslavia. On the basis of the proposals and some thoughts expressed by the assistants, Chief of General Staff, the Chief of General Staff usually ordered the General Staff as a whole to draft such a directive which would then regulate a further performance of the tasks in accordance with the prevailing situation. The sectors in the General Staff and the independent administrations also gave their proposals, their contributions, and the sector for operations and staff activities headed by me was the main agent that did that. And the first operations administration was the part of the sector that actually did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for this directive to be done?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a substantial document, a directive from the Chief of General Staff is an important, substantial document. I'm not trying to diminish the importance of other documents, but this document had to be done in a systematic matter. It was done in five or six days at the end of July, and the Chief of General Staff approved it on the 28th of July, 1998. And it was drafted -- well, some of the parts that pertained to some other sectors were drafted over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That was one of your first major tasks, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes; in essence, yes. I saw this plan, I took part in making it, and I think it was an experience that made it possible for me to carry out this planning function in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 4D137 brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is this directive dated the 28th of July that was done at the level of the General Staff. At the top you can see the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, sector for operations and staff affairs, first administration, that's the hierarchy, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to make it easier for the Chamber to understand, could you please tell us what are the constituent parts of a directive as a rule, what does it consist of? We can see here item 1, the enemy. Could you please tell us what are the elements of the directive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, a directive contains several elements. As you can see here under I you have the assessment of the enemy; II would be tasks of the units; then we have the decision of the commander, the chief, the tasks of the units. And the remaining elements are -- have to do with support. And lastly the logistics support necessary for the execution of the tasks, then command and control, and communications that -- those elements that pertained to the execution of this particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Other witnesses will be talking about this directive, so very briefly, you told us that this directive had two stages. Could you please tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: The name of this plan was Thunder 98. It had two stages. The first stage was called Thunder 1 and the second one was called Thunder 2. As a rule, the execution of the tasks -- well, tasks -- a task is, as a rule, divided into several parts which means that this directive contained this task that tasks should be executed in stages and then following an analysis the -- you should proceed to the next stage of the execution of the task in accordance with the order issued by the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who signed this directive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: It was approved by the Chief of General Staff and that he was the only one who had the power to use the army at this level, so he signed it, he approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 3D702.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this document that you see in front of you, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first document that was submitted to the 3rd Army command on the basis of the directive that was issued. The 3rd Army received its task, and that was to assess and to draft a plan of the use of forces in accordance with the directive in stages and to submit its decision for the justification and approval of the Chief of General Staff in accordance with the decision on the 3rd of August, 1998, at 1100 hours, and that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And so this here where it says: "The approval of the plan of use of forces will be -- I will do this on the 3rd of August," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of an order that the 3rd Army command received, the command assessed the situation and the commander issued his decision on how to use the forces. And his superior officer then verified this plan, and in this case it was the Chief of General Staff. This is very important because it indicates whether the subordinate officer, the subordinate command, actually grasped, understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have problems with translation. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This is of great importance because the officer issuing the order can then assess whether the subordinate officer properly understood the order that was issued and whether he is actually following the spirit of the order at different levels of the chain of command. And if this plan for the use of forces is verified in accordance with the chain of command, then this decision of the commander enters into force and it can then be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 3D703.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell me, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: This document is again drafted on the basis of the directive. It is issued to the commands of the 1st and the 3rd Army, the command of the navy, command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, and the special units command. It was their task again to assess the situation, to elaborate plans for the use of forces in accordance with this directive, and to submit the plan to the General Staff by the 3rd of August at 1000 hours. Since the priority for the execution of this task in accordance with the directive was in the hands of the 3rd Army, the plans of these commands at the General Staff would be studied, analysed, and in accordance with the order of the Chief of General Staff, once the commanders came to defend or to justify their decision in accordance with how they envisaged the use of their forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if we look at the previous document, 3D702, in paragraph 2 it says: "The approval -- I will carry out the approval of the plan of use of forces on the 3rd of August, 1998, at 1100 hours." According to this document that is now in front of you, 3D703, it says the plan of the use of forces is to be submitted by the 3rd of August, 1998, at 1000 hours. Does that mean that the commander of the 3rd Army got his approval for the use -- for the use of forces by the 3rd of August, 1998, at 1100 hours, unlike the commanders of these other formations that are listed here in 3D703?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 3rd Army came to the General Staff, and he faced the people designated by the Chief of General Staff and went on to justify his decision.
